newsitem.title: USA: Race is on to patent cloning techniques.
newsitem.headline: Race is on to patent cloning techniques.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Correspondent

The Scottish biotech company that sponsored historic sheep cloning research is expected to win lucrative international patents for the process, but lawyers predict that rivals are racing to develop new breakthroughs.

PPL Therapeutics Plc delayed announcing the feat until it had already filed a patent application in Britain, lawyers said. Under an international treaty, such action would also preserve the company's right to file for the first patent in the United States.

Because the information in the patent application is confidential, it is unknown whether PPL is seeking patents for more than the cloning process. Lawyers said the company could also be seeking rights to genetically engineered sheep and possibly other animals.
Patent lawyers said this will encourage a race among competitors to develop new and possibly more efficient methods of cloning and to seek related patents, also for other cloned animals.
"It's a fundamental invention ... It's a real sea change and it opens up a lot of issues," Michael Epstein of New York-based law firms Weil, Gotshal & Manges said.
Scottish researchers, led by Dr. Ian Wilmut, a 52-year-old embryologist at the Roslin Institute in Edinburgh, announced last weekend that they had created a lamb using DNA from an adult sheep.

PPL sponsored the research and has applied for the patents. The technology is still clumsy and too imperfect for widespread use, and Wilmut has stressed he intends it to be used on animals only, not people.

While the purpose of the sheep-cloning process was to make theraputic proteins in animal milk, the possibilities are vast and could include creating animals designed to produce drugs and even organs for humans.
Under an international treaty, a company that files for a patent in Britain has one year to file in the United States. The company has the exclusive right to file during that period.

The information contained in the patent application will remain secret unless PPL decides to publicly disclose it or until 18 months have passed and it is released by European authorities, Epstein said.
Information in U.S. applications is made public when the patent is approved, he said.

"The first, the broadest and most valuable patent will most likely go to them (PPL)," Cal Griffith of Cleveland-based Jones, Day, Reavis & Pogue said. "The more valuable part of this invention is the process."
Ken Adamo, also of Jones Day, said, however, that if he were advising PPL, he would suggest seeking a broad patent application that would cover the animal itself as well as the process.
"We'd say 'Claim the non-human mammal, the altered sheep, and then we'll go into the patent office and fight it out as to whether we are entitled to that very broad claim," Adamo said.
In the meantime, research could continue on other species, he said. "We can always throw that in the hopper later on to support broad claim," Adamo added.

Adamo said that competitors may now be trying to use the process to come up with a cloned animal other than a sheep and to race to the patent office with the hopes that PPL will not win a broad claim to non-human mammals.
He said if others should get patents on other cloned animals, it will result in what is known as "blocking patents."

This would mean that the holders of the second patents might not be able to create their animal without permission to use PPL's process. However, PPL would not be able to use its process to make animals other than sheep.
"That's one of the little joys of the American patent system," Adamo said.

"It's all a matter of timing at this point, he said. "How much have the Scots done, what have they put in their application in the U.K. and what has anyone else in the United States done? It does have ...the aspect of a race to it."
